Wet
wet
a. and v. (moistened; in Daniel, of the king wet with the dew of heaven through seven years of beast-madness, and in Job of the poor without shelter)
Old English waet, moist, cognate with water. The Aramaic of Daniel is tseba, to dip or moisten — the same root as the verb used of dipping in dye; the recurring phrase is tal shemayya, the dew of heaven.

Biblical Definition

Five of the six occurrences belong to a single sentence of judgment, repeated four times as decree, warning, fulfilment, and later testimony. The watcher's decree: “let it be wet with the dew of heaven, and let his portion be with the beasts in the grass of the earth” (Daniel 4:15). Daniel's warning to the king: “they shall wet thee with the dew of heaven, and seven times shall pass over thee, till thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will” (Daniel 4:25). The fulfilment: “his body was wet with the dew of heaven, till his hairs were grown like eagles' feathers, and his nails like birds' claws” (Daniel 4:33). And Daniel's reminder to Belshazzar a generation later (Daniel 5:21). The repetition is the point — the purpose clause is stated before the judgment falls, so the reader knows it is corrective and not merely punitive. Nebuchadnezzar wet with dew is a king reduced to the condition of the grass he grazed on, and the end of it is a doxology from his own mouth. Job uses the word of the destitute: “They are wet with the showers of the mountains, and embrace the rock for want of a shelter” (Job 24:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines wet as containing water or other liquid, moist, humid — and as a verb, to fill or moisten with liquid.

expand to see more

WET, a. Containing water, as wet land; or having water or other liquid upon the surface, as a wet table.

2. Rainy; as wet weather; a wet season.

WET, n. Water or wetness; moisture or humidity in considerable degree.

WET, v.t. To fill or moisten with water or other liquid; to sprinkle; to dip in liquor and withdraw.

DEW, n. The water or moisture collected or deposited on or near the surface of the earth in the night.

Key Scripture

Daniel 4:25 — "That they shall drive thee from men, and thy dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field, and they shall make thee to eat grass as oxen, and they shall wet thee with the dew of heaven, and seven times shall pass over thee, till thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will."

Daniel 4:33 — "The same hour was the thing fulfilled upon Nebuchadnezzar: and he was driven from men, and did eat grass as oxen, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven, till his hairs were grown like eagles' feathers, and his nails like birds' claws."

Daniel 4:37 — "Now I Nebuchadnezzar praise and extol and honour the King of heaven, all whose works are truth, and his ways judgment: and those that walk in pride he is able to abase."

Job 24:8 — "They are wet with the showers of the mountains, and embrace the rock for want of a shelter."

Modern Corruption

Nebuchadnezzar's madness is filed under psychiatry and the doctrine drained out of it — that God abases the proud and restores whom He will.

expand to see more

Daniel 4 is regularly handled as a case study, with the king's condition given a clinical name and the narrative treated as a legend built around an illness. The text is not shy about the physical facts — the hair, the nails, the grass, the dew — but it refuses to let them be the explanation. The purpose is stated three times before the event and once after: till thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will. That is not a diagnosis; it is a verdict, and it was published in advance so that the king would recognise it when it came.

The doctrine at stake is the abasement of the proud and the sovereignty of God over kingdoms, and Nebuchadnezzar himself states it in the closing doxology: those that walk in pride he is able to abase. He walked upon his palace and said Is not this great Babylon, that I have built; while the word was in his mouth the sentence fell; and after seven times his understanding returned and he blessed the most High. Reformed readers have always taken this chapter as the plainest scriptural picture of God humbling a man in order to save him, and of a conversion effected by a providence no counsellor would have prescribed. Job 24:8 keeps the other end in view: the same dew and rain fall on the poor who have no shelter, and God sees them too.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Aramaic tseba, to moisten or dip — Daniel 4:15, 25, 33; tal, dew — the recurring phrase; Hebrew ratab, to be moist — Job 24:8.

expand to see more

Aramaic tseba — to dip, to moisten; the verb in every Daniel occurrence.

Aramaic tal shemayya — the dew of heaven; the phrase repeated four times in the judgment.

Aramaic illaya — the most High; the title used throughout the chapter, and the point of the whole judgment.

Hebrew ratab — to be moist, wet; Job 24:8 of the destitute in the mountains.

Old English waet — moist; cognate with water.

Usage

"“They shall wet thee with the dew of heaven” — the sentence announced before it fell."

"“Till thou know that the most High ruleth” — the stated purpose of the madness."

"“Those that walk in pride he is able to abase” — the king's own conclusion."
